A useful identity is

\[
(x+1)(x-4)^2=x^3-7x^2+8x+16,
\]

so

\[
f_q(x)=(x+1)(x-4)^2+(q-8)x.
\]

---

### 1. Show that for every \(q>8\), there is exactly one real root.

For \(x>0\),

\[
(x+1)(x-4)^2\ge 0
\]

and

\[
(q-8)x>0.
\]

Thus

\[
f_q(x)>0 \qquad (x>0).
\]

Also \(f_q(0)=16>0\), so there are no nonnegative real roots.

For \(x<0\),

\[
f_q'(x)=3x^2-14x+q.
\]

Since \(x<0\) and \(q>8\),

\[
3x^2\ge 0,\qquad -14x>0,\qquad q>0,
\]

so

\[
f_q'(x)>0.
\]

Hence \(f_q\) is strictly increasing on \((-\infty,0)\). Since

\[
\lim_{x\to-\infty}f_q(x)=-\infty
\]

and

\[
f_q(0)=16>0,
\]

there is exactly one real root in \((-\infty,0)\). Therefore, for every \(q>8\), the cubic has exactly one real root.

So \(p=8\) works.

---

### 2. Show that no smaller \(p\) can work.

Now suppose \(q<8\). Then

\[
f_q(-1)=8-q>0
\]

and

\[
f_q(4)=4q-32<0.
\]

Also,

\[
\lim_{x\to-\infty}f_q(x)=-\infty
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lim_{x\to\infty}f_q(x)=\infty.
\]

Therefore, by the Intermediate Value Theorem:

- there is a root in \((-\infty,-1)\),
- there is a root in \((-1,4)\),
- there is a root in \((4,\infty)\).

Thus for every \(q<8\), the cubic has three real roots.

If \(p<8\), we can choose \(q\) such that \(p<q<8\). Then the cubic has three real roots, so the required condition fails.

Hence the minimum possible value of \(p\) is

\[
\boxed{8}.
\]
